sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Break the word like Legos: 'my/o' is the muscle piece and 'cardi/o' is the heart piece. Snap them together and you get 'heart muscle,' which is the thick, squeezing middle layer that does the actual pumping. The other choices all end the same way but start with pieces that mean inside, around, or on top of, so they are membranes, not muscle.

### Question 2

Think of '-emia' as a label that says 'something is going on in the blood.' When you see it at the end of a word, the front part tells you what that something is. In anemia, the front part means 'not enough,' so the whole word means 'a blood condition where you don't have enough' of the red, oxygen-carrying stuff.

### Question 3

Each blood cell name tells you its color or job. 'Leuk/o' means white, and white blood cells are the body's little soldiers that fight germs. The red ones (erythr/o) carry oxygen, and the clot ones (thromb/o) plug up cuts, so only the white soldiers fit the job of fighting infection.

### Question 4

The speed of the word lives in the front piece. 'Brady-' is the slow one and 'tachy-' is the fast one (think of a taxi zooming). Since '-cardia' just means 'heart condition,' the front piece 'brady-' is what tells you the heart is going slow.

### Question 5

Both words start with 'hem/o' for blood, so the ending decides what happens. '-stasis' means 'stay put / stop,' so hemostasis is blood stopping (a good thing when you're cut). '-rrhage' means 'bursting out,' so hemorrhage is blood pouring out too much. Same start, opposite endings, opposite meanings.

### Question 6

The middle of the word tells you which pipe is in trouble. 'Arteri/o' points to arteries (the pipes carrying blood away from the heart) and 'phleb/o' points to veins (the pipes carrying blood back). So one word is about arteries and the other about veins, even though both are blood vessels.

### Question 7

Keep the heart part ('cardi/o') and just change the ending to change what's wrong with it. '-megaly' means 'big' and '-itis' means 'sore and swollen.' Swap the 'big' ending for the 'swollen' ending and you go from 'big heart' to 'inflamed heart.'

### Question 8

'-ectomy' is the 'take it out' ending, like when a surgeon removes something. The front piece 'thromb/o' means a clot, which is a blood plug. Put them together and it means a doctor took the clot out, not made one or just looked at it.

### Question 9

'Echo' is the bouncing-sound part, like when your voice bounces back in a canyon. Machines bounce sound off the heart and use the echoes to draw a picture, and '-graphy' means 'making a recording or picture.' So the word means taking a sound-picture of the heart.

### Question 10

The ending '-cytosis' means 'too many cells,' and its opposite '-penia' means 'too few.' Since 'leuk/o' means white cells, leukocytosis is 'too many white soldiers,' which the body often makes when it's fighting off germs. So the word points to more white cells, not fewer.

### Question 11

Both words mean 'the heart part is swollen and sore' because they end in '-itis.' The front piece is like an address label: 'peri-' means the bag around the heart and 'endo-' means the lining inside the heart. Swap the label and you send the swelling to the wrong place, even though the problem type stays the same.

### Question 12

This word is a factory word. 'Hemat/o' means blood and '-poiesis' means 'making,' so it means the body building brand-new blood cells, mostly inside your bones. The wrong answers use other real endings that mean breaking down, stopping, or a lump, so watching the exact ending is what gets you the right meaning.
